newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan battles oil slicks but weather a problem.
newsitem.headline: Japan battles oil slicks but weather a problem.

text.p: Japanese ships on Sunday tried to break up slicks from one of the biggest oil spills ever to threaten the nation's coast, but efforts were hampered by bad weather, officials said.

An estimated 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of heavy oil have escaped from a ruptured Russian tanker which broke up in the Sea of Japan off the northern coast on Thursday, prompting the Maritime Safety Agency to set up a special task force to handle the potential crisis.

A spokesman for the maritime agency said there were two major groups of oil slicks, with the closer group about 70 km (45 miles) off the coast of the main island of Honshu as of Sunday evening. It contained slicks of up to 10 km (five miles) in length, he said.

The spill is the second-largest ever to pose a threat to the Japanese coast. In 1971, 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata in northern Japan.
Efforts had been hampered on Friday and Saturday by continued strong winds and heavy seas that caused the freighter to split in two. Most of the vessel is now under water.
The flotilla of 10 ships spent the day dropping detergent and churning up the water to try to break up the slicks.
But their efforts were again curtailed with the return of bad weather in the area.

The Russian-registered Nakhodka was built 26 years ago and authorities said the age of the ship, which was heading for Russia from China, was probably a factor in the vessel breaking apart in the rough seas.
The 31 crew from the tanker were rescued but the captain was still missing. Officials said there was almost no hope that he had survived.
With winds up to 50 Km (30 miles) per hour, the maritime agency fears the oil could reach the coast in a few days.
Officials are also worried about the oil still aboard in unruptured tanks. The vessel was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of grade C heavy oil.
The agency hopes to tow the bow of the ship, which is partly submerged, back to port.
Any oil washing to shore would be a blow to the region. Shellfish are a speciality of the 300 Km (180 mile) swathe of picturesque coastline, which is dotted with fishing villages.

"We have alerted the shellfish, seaweed and other agricultural producers' organisations along the coast that the slicks are headed for, but we don't know if there's anything they can do to prevent the oil hitting the shores," the maritime agency spokesman said.
Fishing remains a major industry in Japan. Seafood is a mainstay of the Japanese diet and closely tied to its history and culture.
Despite its heavy reliance on imported oil, Japan has avoided any of the large-scale environmental disasters that have hit elsewhere.
